title: Spontaneous emission of light by non-equilibrium phonons
authors: J. Plo, P. Valvin, M. Moret, T. Taliercio, J. Batista, T. Sohier, A. Vasanelli, C. Sirtori, B. Gil, W. Desrat, G. Cassabois
abstract: When a system is brought out of equilibrium by an external excitation, its relaxation to thermodynamic equilibrium generates phonons. These non-equilibrium phonons degrade via cascaded anharmonic decay processes, progressively leading to a thermal population of phonons following a Bose-Einstein distribution at the system temperature. Preceding heat dissipation by convection, conduction and incandescence, this early phase of the relaxation dynamics is commonly assumed to be exclusively non-radiative. Here, we demonstrate that the radiative emission by phonons can be an efficient relaxation pathway competing with the intrinsic anharmonic decay. Optical spectroscopy under femtosecond two-photon excitation in boron nitride unveils a photoluminescence signal in the mid-infrared spectral range, stemming from the spontaneous emission of light by non-equilibrium phonons. This observation of non-thermal radiation from phonons introduces a new paradigm for out-of-equilibrium physics, mid-infrared optics, and thermal management.
summary: This research demonstrates that spontaneous light emission from non-equilibrium phonons can be a major energy dissipation channel in materials like boron nitride. By using ultrafast spectroscopy and theory, the authors distinguish this radiative process from purely anharmonic decay, opening new avenues for understanding out-of-equilibrium physics and infrared optoelectronics.
main_problem: The study investigates spontaneous light emission from non-equilibrium phonons, proposing this radiative decay as a significant relaxation pathway competing with intrinsic anharmonic phonon decay processes.
main_result: The authors report the first detection of mid-infrared photoluminescence originating from these non-equilibrium phonons in boron nitride, demonstrating that radiation can be an efficient out-of-equilibrium energy dissipation mechanism.
method: The work combines ultrafast optical spectroscopy (femtosecond two-photon excitation) with theoretical calculations (DFT) to model phonon decay pathways and measure spectral signatures.
model_or_system: The physical system is boron nitride (BN), particularly rhombohedral BN microcrystallites, which are used as a platform for observing light-matter interactions under non-equilibrium conditions. The physics involves the relaxation of excited states generating non-thermal phonon populations.
key_observables: Photoluminescence (PL) signal in the mid-infrared spectral range ($\lambda \sim 7 \mu	ext{m}$), excitonic PL ($\lambda \sim 215 	ext{ nm}$), and the partial temperature ($eT$) derived from power dependence.
important_parameters: Femtosecond excitation timescales, cryogenic temperatures ($T \sim 25$ K), and spectral regimes distinguishing one-phonon (strong coupling) vs. two-phonon (weak coupling) decay.
main_assumptions: The analysis distinguishes between intrinsic (two-phonon) and extrinsic (one-phonon) radiative decay based on established coupling regimes, and the $eT$ estimate assumes negligible exciton collisional broadening.
figures_summary: Figures show IR-UV dual-band imaging contrasting phononic PL ($\lambda \sim 7 \mu	ext{m}$) with excitonic PL ($\lambda \sim 215 	ext{ nm}$), and power dependence measurements confirming Auger processes and the transition between one-phonon and two-phonon decay regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from initial experimental observation of MIR photoluminescence in BN, to detailed analysis distinguishing radiative pathways (one- vs. two-phonon), culminating in theoretical calculations matching these intrinsic two-phonon decay signatures.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium dynamics and energy relaxation mechanisms beyond simple thermal models, which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems where coupling to a bath (phonons) dictates the system's evolution.
